newsitem.title: UK: Russia chemical stocks seen posing danger for years.
newsitem.headline: Russia chemical stocks seen posing danger for years.

text.p: Russia's chemical weapons stockpiles will remain a hazard for many years to come because Moscow cannot afford to destroy them, the monthly Janes's Intelligence Review said.
An article in the June issue, obtained on Friday ahead of publication, said efforts to destroy the stocks were also being hampered by increasingly effective environmental protests.
Official sources say Russia has around 40,000 tonnes of nerve and blister agents which need to be destroyed in a process officially known as chemical demilitarisation.
Russia signed the Chemical Weapons Convention in 1993, committing itself to eliminating the stocks, but parliament has postponed approval of the treaty despite pressure from President Boris Yeltsin.
Legislators argue that Russia needs more time and Western financial aid to destroy the weapons and Janes's said there was little prospect of an early breakthrough.

"At a time when Russia is struggling to fund military reform, weapons development and other programmes vital to national security, the prospect of fulfilling scheduled chemical demilitarisation plans while ensuring the required social and environmental safeguards is virtually non-existent."
The review said local communities unhappy about the idea of chemical weapons destruction sites being built next door were mounting ever more effective opposition.

"As the federal government continues to cede more authority to regions through power-sharing arrangements, chemical weapon destruction projects are likely to be held hostage to a wide range of demands from the local population," it said.

To make matters worse, nationalistic parliamentarians were starting to link the chemical demilitarisation programme to NATO expansion and the implementation of strategic nuclear disarmament treaties, Janes's said.

"This could mean that, with any delay expected to increase the total costs of the chemical demilitarisation programme, Russia's chemical weapons stockpile will remain a security and environmental hazard for the forseeable future."
The review said the amount of money earmarked in the Russian budget for chemical demilitarisation was in any case woefully inadequate.
The 1997 budget provided 120 billion roubles ($21 million) while the actual sum needed was around 1.2 trillion roubles ($210 million).
"The realities of Russia's current economic siutation have led to general agreement that Moscow cannot bear the costs itself and that external assistance is urgently needed," Janes's said.
The review said Moscow should consider approaching the World Bank and other potential foreign donors to find enough money to at least start the process of destroying the stockpiles.
